claim: TFIIIC binds directly to the amino-terminal transcriptional regulatory domain of MYCN.
source: Here, we show that TFIIIC, an architectural protein complex that controls the three-dimensional chromatin organisation at its target sites, binds directly to the amino-terminal transcriptional regulatory domain of MYCN.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: TFIIIC has no discernible role in MYCN-dependent gene expression and transcription elongation.
source: Surprisingly, TFIIIC has no discernible role in MYCN-dependent gene expression and transcription elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D showing no significant effects on gene expression.

claim: MYCN and TFIIIC preferentially bind to promoters with paused RNAPII.
source: Instead, MYCN and TFIIIC preferentially bind to promoters with paused RNAPII and globally limit the accumulation of non-phosphorylated RNAPII at promoters.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing enhanced TFIIIC5 association with promoters in the presence of DRB, which stabilizes paused RNAPII (Figure 2F).

claim: MYCN and TFIIIC globally limit the accumulation of non-phosphorylated RNAPII at promoters.
source: Instead, MYCN and TFIIIC preferentially bind to promoters with paused RNAPII and globally limit the accumulation of non-phosphorylated RNAPII at promoters.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data in Figure 2A-C showing that activation of MYCN causes a global decrease in promoter association of non-phosphorylated RNAPII, and depletion of TFIIIC5 abrogates this effect.

claim: MYCN broadly participates in hubs of active promoters.
source: Consistent with its ubiquitous role in transcription, MYCN broadly participates in hubs of active promoters.
evidence: This is supported by pLHiChIP data showing thousands of MYCN interactions connecting promoters (Figure 3A-E).

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC increases MYCN localisation to promoter hubs.
source: Depletion of TFIIIC further increases MYCN localisation to these hubs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by spLHiChIP experiments showing that depletion of TFIIIC5 strongly increased the number of chromatin interactions of MYCN (Figure 4E and F).

claim: The increase in MYCN localization to hubs upon TFIIIC depletion correlates with a failure of the nuclear exosome to localise to active promoters.
source: This increase correlates with a failure of the nuclear exosome and BRCA1, both of which are involved in nascent RNA degradation, to localise to active promoters.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN experiments showing that depletion of TFIIIC5 strongly decreased the association of EXOSC5 with regions around the TSS (Figure 5B).

claim: The increase in MYCN localization to hubs upon TFIIIC depletion correlates with a failure of BRCA1 to localise to active promoters.
source: This increase correlates with a failure of the nuclear exosome and BRCA1, both of which are involved in nascent RNA degradation, to localise to active promoters.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP experiments showing that depletion of TFIIIC5 abrogated BRCA1 recruitment by MYCN at all promoters tested (Figure 5C).

claim: MYCN and TFIIIC exert a censoring function in early transcription that limits promoter accumulation of inactive RNAPII.
source: Our data suggest that MYCN and TFIIIC exert an censoring function in early transcription that limits promoter accumulation of inactive RNAPII and facilitates promoter-proximal degradation of nascent RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including the effects on non-phosphorylated RNAPII accumulation and the requirement for TFIIIC in exosome and BRCA1 localization.

claim: MYCN and TFIIIC facilitate promoter-proximal degradation of nascent RNA.
source: Our data suggest that MYCN and TFIIIC exert an censoring function in early transcription that limits promoter accumulation of inactive RNAPII and facilitates promoter-proximal degradation of nascent RNA.
evidence: This is supported by data showing TFIIIC is required for association of the nuclear exosome and BRCA1 with promoters (Figure 5B-C).

claim: The amino-terminal region of recombinant MYCN binds to TFIIIC in pull-down experiments performed with cell lysates.
source: TFIIIC is present in MYCN immunoprecipitates and the amino-terminal region of recombinant MYCN binds to TFIIIC in pull-down experiments performed with cell lysates (Büchel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: All six subunits of the TFIIIC complex were recovered in pull-down experiments with FLAG-tagged MYCN amino acids 2-137.
source: Performing pull-down experiments with cell lysates and immobilised FLAG-tagged MYCN, we recovered all six subunits of the TFIIIC complex in the eluate along with the FLAG-tagged MYCN construct, demonstrating that TFIIIC can bind to the amino-terminal region of MYCN (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TFIIIC is composed of two subcomplexes, designated TauA (τA) and TauB (τB), each comprising three of the six subunits.
source: TFIIIC is composed of two subcomplexes, designated TauA (τA) and TauB (τB), each comprising three of the six subunits.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TFIIIC structure.

claim: The τB complex was too unstable to be isolated.
source: We first attempted co-expression of FLAG-MYCN with individual subcomplexes, but the τB complex was too unstable to be isolated, and so we focused on the stable τA complex.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work.

claim: MYCN binds directly to the τA subcomplex of TFIIIC.
source: To test whether MYCN binds directly to τA, we purified MYCN and the τA complex separately (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B) and then mixed the purified preparations (Figure 1B–D). In gel filtration experiments, the isolated MYCN protein eluted with a molecular weight of around 50 kDa, whereas a fraction of MYCN eluted with a much larger molecular weight together with the τA complex when both were mixed (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gel filtration and native mass spectrometry experiments (Figure 1B-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).

claim: The MYCN amino-terminal region and the τA subcomplex of TFIIIC form a stable complex with a 1:1:1:1 stoichiometry.
source: Native mass spectrometry (Tamara et al., 2022) showed the molecular weight of this complex to be 204.7 kDa, very close to the sum of the molecular weights of a 1:1:1:1 complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D). We concluded that the MYCN amino-terminal region and the τA subcomplex of TFIIIC form a stable complex with each other in solution.
evidence: This is demonstrated by native mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC2 or TFIIIC3 attenuated proliferation of SH-EP-MYCN-ER cells under control conditions.
source: Under control conditions, depletion of TFIIIC2 or TFIIIC3 attenuated proliferation, whereas depletion of the small TFIIIC5 subunit had little effect.
evidence: This is shown by growth curve data in Figure 1E.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC5 had little effect on proliferation of SH-EP-MYCN-ER cells under control conditions.
source: Under control conditions, depletion of TFIIIC2 or TFIIIC3 attenuated proliferation, whereas depletion of the small TFIIIC5 subunit had little effect.
evidence: This is shown by growth curve data in Figure 1E.

claim: Addition of 4-OHT greatly enhanced the inhibitory effect of depletion of each TFIIIC subunit on cell proliferation.
source: Addition of 4-OHT had little effect by itself, but greatly enhanced the inhibitory effect of depletion of each subunit (Figure 1E), suggesting that TFIIIC has both general and MYCN-specific roles in neuroblastoma cell proliferation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth curve data in Figure 1E.

claim: TFIIIC has both general and MYCN-specific roles in neuroblastoma cell proliferation.
source: Addition of 4-OHT had little effect by itself, but greatly enhanced the inhibitory effect of depletion of each subunit (Figure 1E), suggesting that TFIIIC has both general and MYCN-specific roles in neuroblastoma cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of TFIIIC depletion with and without MYCN activation.

claim: MYCN promotes pause release and MYCN's effect on elongation correlates with its effects on gene expression.
source: First, MYCN promotes pause release and MYCN's effect on elongation correlates with its effects on gene expression (Herold et al., 2019; Rahl et al., 2010; Walz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activation of MYCN uniformly reduces RNAPII occupancy at all active promoters.
source: At the same time, activation of MYCN uniformly reduces RNAPII occupancy at all active promoters; this correlates with a reduced accumulation of promoter-proximal R-loops, suggesting that MYCN limits the accumulation of RNAPII at promoters that is impaired in productive elongation and/or splicing (Herold et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Activation of MYCN caused a global decrease in promoter association of non-phosphorylated RNAPII.
source: Visual inspection of multiple individual genes (Figure 2A) and global analyses (Figure 2B and C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) showed that activation of MYCN caused a global decrease in promoter association of non-phosphorylated RNAPII.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Addition of 4-OHT had no effect on non-phosphorylated RNAPII in SH-EP cells that do not express an MYCN-ER chimera.
source: A control ChIP-seq experiment established that addition of 4-OHT had no such effect in SH-EP cells that do not express an MYCN-ER chimera, demonstrating that the reduction is due to activation of MYCN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This control experiment is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MYCN promoted an increase in transcription elongation as documented by pSer2-RNAPII occupancy at the transcription end site (TES).
source: At the same time, MYCN promoted an increase in transcription elongation as best documented by pSer2-RNAPII occupancy at the transcription end site (TES) (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq data in Figure 2A and C.

claim: The MYCN-dependent increase in pSer2-RNAPII at TES was most pronounced on MYCN-activated genes.
source: This increase was most pronounced on MYCN-activated genes.
evidence: This is shown in the ChIP-seq data analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: The MYCN-dependent increase in pSer2-RNAPII at TES correlated closely with MYCN-dependent changes in gene expression.
source: Comparison with RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data showed that it correlated closely with MYCN-dependent changes in gene expression (Figure 2D).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 2D comparing ChIP-Rx and RNA-seq data.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC5 abrogated the MYCN-dependent decrease in chromatin association of non-phosphorylated RNAPII.
source: Depletion of TFIIIC5 abrogated the MYCN-dependent decrease in chromatin association of non-phosphorylated RNAPII but had no effect on MYCN-dependent changes in transcription elongation (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC5 had no effect on MYCN-dependent changes in transcription elongation.
source: Depletion of TFIIIC5 abrogated the MYCN-dependent decrease in chromatin association of non-phosphorylated RNAPII but had no effect on MYCN-dependent changes in transcription elongation (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Neither depletion of TFIIIC3 nor of TFIIIC5 had significant effects on basal gene expression.
source: Consistent with these observations, RNA-seq showed that neither depletion of TFIIIC3 nor of TFIIIC5 had significant effects on either basal gene expression or MYCN-dependent changes in steady-state mRNA levels (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by RNA-seq data in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Neither depletion of TFIIIC3 nor of TFIIIC5 had significant effects on MYCN-dependent changes in steady-state mRNA levels.
source: Consistent with these observations, RNA-seq showed that neither depletion of TFIIIC3 nor of TFIIIC5 had significant effects on either basal gene expression or MYCN-dependent changes in steady-state mRNA levels (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by RNA-seq data in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Activation of MYCN globally enhanced TFIIIC5 association with regions surrounding active transcription start sites.
source: Inspection of individual genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and average density plots of all active promoters (Figure 2F) showed that activation of MYCN globally enhanced TFIIIC5 association with regions surrounding active transcription start sites, consistent with previous observations (Büchel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Addition of DRB increased TFIIIC5 association with active promoters.
source: Addition of DRB increased TFIIIC5 association with active promoters and the combination of MYCN activation and DRB had a strong additive effect, arguing that MYCN preferentially recruits TFIIIC5 to promoters with paused RNAPII.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq data in Figure 2F.

claim: The combination of MYCN activation and DRB had a strong additive effect on TFIIIC5 association with promoters.
source: Addition of DRB increased TFIIIC5 association with active promoters and the combination of MYCN activation and DRB had a strong additive effect, arguing that MYCN preferentially recruits TFIIIC5 to promoters with paused RNAPII.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-seq data in Figure 2F and supports the inference that MYCN recruits TFIIIC5 to paused promoters.

claim: MYCN preferentially recruits TFIIIC5 to promoters with paused RNAPII.
source: Addition of DRB increased TFIIIC5 association with active promoters and the combination of MYCN activation and DRB had a strong additive effect, arguing that MYCN preferentially recruits TFIIIC5 to promoters with paused RNAPII.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effect of MYCN and DRB on TFIIIC5 association with promoters.

claim: MYCN pLHiChIP identified a total of 4591 distinct binary interactions involving MYCN.
source: The pLHiChIP data analysis revealed a total of 4591 distinct binary interactions involving MYCN (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is the result of pLHiChIP data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 1277 out of the 4591 MYCN anchors (28%) were positioned on RNAPII promoters.
source: Remarkably, our analysis revealed that 1277 out of the 4591 MYCN anchors (28%) were positioned on RNAPII promoters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from the analysis of pLHiChIP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 864 out of the 4591 MYCN interactions (19%) exhibited connections between promoters and either exonic or intronic sequences.
source: Furthermore, 864 out of the 4591 MYCN interactions (19%) exhibited connections between promoters and either exonic or intronic sequences, consistent with previous observations showing that MYCN binding sites are often located within transcribed regions (Büchel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is from pLHiChIP data analysis and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: MYCN interactions were observed between promoters and SINE repetitive elements (647/4591; 14%).
source: Additionally, MYCN interactions were observed between promoters and SINE repetitive elements (647/4591; 14%) including interactions with tRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is from pLHiChIP data analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: MYCN interactions between promoters or gene bodies and enhancers accounted for 453 out of the 4591 interactions (10%).
source: We also observed interactions between promoters or gene bodies and enhancers, accounting for 453 out of the 4591 interactions (10%).
evidence: This is from pLHiChIP data analysis.

claim: Significantly more MYCN bound to promoters that participated in three-dimensional MYCN interactions than to MYCN-bound promoters without such interactions.
source: This showed that significantly more MYCN and RNAPII bound to promoters that participated in such interactions and that these promoters were more active than MYCN-bound promoters without such interactions, although the latter difference was small Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 3C comparing promoters with and without MYCN interactions.

claim: Significantly more RNAPII bound to promoters that participated in three-dimensional MYCN interactions than to MYCN-bound promoters without such interactions.
source: This showed that significantly more MYCN and RNAPII bound to promoters that participated in such interactions and that these promoters were more active than MYCN-bound promoters without such interactions, although the latter difference was small Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: Promoters that participated in MYCN interactions were more active than MYCN-bound promoters without such interactions, although the difference was small.
source: This showed that significantly more MYCN and RNAPII bound to promoters that participated in such interactions and that these promoters were more active than MYCN-bound promoters without such interactions, although the latter difference was small Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 3C comparing mRNA and 4sU levels.

claim: MYCN participated in three-dimensional promoter hubs of different sizes, with the largest connecting up to 34 promoters and 10 enhancers.
source: We next used the binary interactions as a starting point to reconstruct interaction networks. This showed that MYCN participated in three-dimensional promoter hubs of different sizes (Figure 3D), with the largest connecting up to 34 promoters and 10 enhancers (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by network reconstruction analysis in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The number of promoters in the largest MYCN hubs (up to 34) is consistent with published estimates.
source: This number of promoters is consistent with published estimates (Palacio and Taatjes, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Promoters contained in large MYCN hubs are highly enriched in genes encoding ribosomal proteins and ribosome biogenesis genes transcribed by RNAPII.
source: Functional annotation of the promoters that are contained in these large hubs showed that they are highly enriched in genes encoding ribosomal proteins and ribosome biogenesis genes transcribed by RNAPII (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is shown by functional annotation analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: TFIIIC pLHiChIP identified a total of 3499 binary non-contiguous interactions for TFIIIC.
source: Specifically, these analyses identified a total of 3499 binary non-contiguous interactions for TFIIIC.
evidence: This is the result of TFIIIC pLHiChIP data analysis.

claim: 31% of TFIIIC interactions connected a promoter or the gene body of an RNAPII-transcribed gene to a SINE repetitive element.
source: Comparison to RNAPII ChIP-seq data showed that 31% of these interactions connected a promoter or the gene body of an RNAPII-transcribed gene to a SINE repetitive element (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is from TFIIIC pLHiChIP data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 1107 out of 4591 MYCN interactions shared one (1075) or both (32) anchors with TFIIIC-containing interactions.
source: Importantly, 1107 out of 4591 MYCN interactions shared one (1075) or both (32) anchors with TFIIIC-containing interactions arguing that both proteins participate in common hubs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is from comparison of MYCN and TFIIIC pLHiChIP data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MYCN and TFIIIC participate in common hubs.
source: Importantly, 1107 out of 4591 MYCN interactions shared one (1075) or both (32) anchors with TFIIIC-containing interactions arguing that both proteins participate in common hubs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the overlap of MYCN and TFIIIC interactions.

claim: A significant percentage of the interactions shared between MYCN and TFIIIC contained an E-box in one anchor and A- or B-boxes in the other anchor sequence.
source: A significant percentage of the interactions that are shared between MYCN and TFIIIC contained an E-box in one anchor and A- or B-boxes, which are bound by TFIIIC, in the other anchor sequence, arguing that MYCN and TFIIIC can participate in the same interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by motif analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MYCN and TFIIIC can participate in the same interactions.
source: A significant percentage of the interactions that are shared between MYCN and TFIIIC contained an E-box in one anchor and A- or B-boxes, which are bound by TFIIIC, in the other anchor sequence, arguing that MYCN and TFIIIC can participate in the same interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of both MYCN and TFIIIC binding motifs in shared interactions.

claim: Most interactions that are shared by MYCN and TFIIIC connected promoters to other promoters, to gene bodies or to SINE elements.
source: Most interactions that are shared by MYCN and TFIIIC connected promoters to other promoters, to gene bodies or to SINE elements.
evidence: This is from analysis of shared MYCN and TFIIIC interactions shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TFIIIC5 anchors without overlapping MYCN loops did not show an enrichment for promoter interactions.
source: Conversely, TFIIIC5 anchors without overlapping MYCN loops ('TFIIIC5 only') did not show an enrichment for promoter interactions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown by the analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC5 strongly increased the number of chromatin interactions of MYCN.
source: These experiments showed that depletion of TFIIIC5 strongly increased the number of chromatin interactions of MYCN, arguing that association with TFIIIC antagonises MYCN participation in promoter hubs (Figure 4E and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spLHiChIP data in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Association with TFIIIC antagonises MYCN participation in promoter hubs.
source: These experiments showed that depletion of TFIIIC5 strongly increased the number of chromatin interactions of MYCN, arguing that association with TFIIIC antagonises MYCN participation in promoter hubs (Figure 4E and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TFIIIC5 depletion increases MYCN interactions.

claim: Expression of MYCN moderately decreased the frequency of three-dimensional interactions of TFIIIC5.
source: HiChIP experiments performed for TFIIIC5 showed that expression of MYCN moderately and blockade of pause release by DRB strongly decreased the frequency of three-dimensional interactions of TFIIIC5 (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is shown by TFIIIC5 spLHiChIP data in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Blockade of pause release by DRB strongly decreased the frequency of three-dimensional interactions of TFIIIC5.
source: HiChIP experiments performed for TFIIIC5 showed that expression of MYCN moderately and blockade of pause release by DRB strongly decreased the frequency of three-dimensional interactions of TFIIIC5 (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is shown by TFIIIC5 spLHiChIP data in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Interactions of TFIIIC5 with promoters, gene bodies, and SINE elements were all decreased upon incubation of cells with DRB.
source: Stratification showed that interactions of TFIIIC5 with promoters, gene bodies, and SINE elements were all decreased upon incubation of cells with DRB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), arguing that MYCN/TFIIIC5-bound genes are not part of three-dimensional promoter hubs.
evidence: This is shown by the stratified analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MYCN/TFIIIC5-bound genes are not part of three-dimensional promoter hubs.
source: Stratification showed that interactions of TFIIIC5 with promoters, gene bodies, and SINE elements were all decreased upon incubation of cells with DRB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), arguing that MYCN/TFIIIC5-bound genes are not part of three-dimensional promoter hubs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DRB decreases TFIIIC5 interactions.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC3 caused significant increases in intron retention and exon skipping.
source: This showed that depletion of TFIIIC3 caused significant increases in intron retention and exon skipping, evidence of aberrant splicing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by rMATS analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Most splicing alterations caused by TFIIIC3 depletion occurred in downstream exons and were not observed for TFIIIC5.
source: However, most of these alterations occurred in downstream exons, and were not observed for TFIIIC5.
evidence: This is from rMATS analysis of splicing changes.

claim: Expression of MYCN weakened the splicing error effect of TFIIIC3 depletion.
source: Furthermore, expression of MYCN weakened this effect for TFIIIC3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B), arguing that it does account for the requirement for TFIIIC function in MYCN-expressing cells.
evidence: This is shown by rMATS analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Activation of MYCN enhanced the proximity between TFIIIC5 and total RNAPII.
source: Consistent with the ChIP-seq data, activation of MYCN enhanced the proximity between TFIIIC5 and total RNAPII and depletion of TFIIIC5 reduced the signal, confirming the specificity of the assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by PLA data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC5 reduced the PLA signal between TFIIIC5 and total RNAPII.
source: Consistent with the ChIP-seq data, activation of MYCN enhanced the proximity between TFIIIC5 and total RNAPII and depletion of TFIIIC5 reduced the signal, confirming the specificity of the assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by PLA data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Activation of MYCN and depletion of TFIIIC5 had only weak effects on the proximity of RNAPII with NELFE.
source: Activation of MYCN and depletion of TFIIIC5 had only weak effects on the proximity of RNAPII with NELFE, which associates with pausing RNAPII.
evidence: This is shown by PLA data in Figure 5A.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC5 either alone or in combination with MYCN activation enhanced the proximity of RNAPII with PP2A.
source: Similarly, depletion of TFIIIC5 either alone or in combination with MYCN activation enhanced the proximity of RNAPII with PP2A, which is recruited to promoters via its interaction with the integrator termination complex (Cossa et al., 2021; Vervoort et al., 2021), and with PNUTS, a targeting subunit of PP1 that is globally involved in termination (Figure 5A; Cortazar et al., 2019; Estell et al., 2023; Landsverk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is shown by PLA data in Figure 5A.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC5 either alone or in combination with MYCN activation enhanced the proximity of RNAPII with PNUTS.
source: Similarly, depletion of TFIIIC5 either alone or in combination with MYCN activation enhanced the proximity of RNAPII with PP2A, which is recruited to promoters via its interaction with the integrator termination complex (Cossa et al., 2021; Vervoort et al., 2021), and with PNUTS, a targeting subunit of PP1 that is globally involved in termination (Figure 5A; Cortazar et al., 2019; Estell et al., 2023; Landsverk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is shown by PLA data in Figure 5A.

claim: PP2A is recruited to promoters via its interaction with the integrator termination complex.
source: Similarly, depletion of TFIIIC5 either alone or in combination with MYCN activation enhanced the proximity of RNAPII with PP2A, which is recruited to promoters via its interaction with the integrator termination complex (Cossa et al., 2021; Vervoort et al., 2021), and with PNUTS, a targeting subunit of PP1 that is globally involved in termination (Figure 5A; Cortazar et al., 2019; Estell et al., 2023; Landsverk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: PNUTS is a targeting subunit of PP1 that is globally involved in termination.
source: Similarly, depletion of TFIIIC5 either alone or in combination with MYCN activation enhanced the proximity of RNAPII with PP2A, which is recruited to promoters via its interaction with the integrator termination complex (Cossa et al., 2021; Vervoort et al., 2021), and with PNUTS, a targeting subunit of PP1 that is globally involved in termination (Figure 5A; Cortazar et al., 2019; Estell et al., 2023; Landsverk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC5 strongly decreased the association of EXOSC5 with regions around the TSS, both in control and in MYCN-expressing cells.
source: In contrast, CUT&RUN experiments using antibodies-directed EXOSC5, a core structural subunit of the exosome (Kilchert et al., 2016), showed that depletion of TFIIIC5 strongly decreased the association of EXOSC5 with regions around the TSS, both in control and in MYCN-expressing cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by CUT&RUN data in Figure 5B.

claim: EXOSC5 is a core structural subunit of the exosome.
source: In contrast, CUT&RUN experiments using antibodies-directed EXOSC5, a core structural subunit of the exosome (Kilchert et al., 2016), showed that depletion of TFIIIC5 strongly decreased the association of EXOSC5 with regions around the TSS, both in control and in MYCN-expressing cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Only low amounts of BRCA1 were found at core promoters in SH-EP cells.
source: Consistent with our previous observations, only low amount of BRCA1 were found at core promoter in SH-EP cells and that induction of MYCN recruited BRCA1 to all tested promoters (Herold et al., 2019).
evidence: This is consistent with previous observations cited.

claim: Induction of MYCN recruited BRCA1 to all tested promoters.
source: Consistent with our previous observations, only low amount of BRCA1 were found at core promoter in SH-EP cells and that induction of MYCN recruited BRCA1 to all tested promoters (Herold et al., 2019).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP data in Figure 5C and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: Depletion of TFIIIC5 abrogated BRCA1 recruitment by MYCN at all promoters tested.
source: Depletion of TFIIIC5 had variable effects on the presence of BRCA1 by itself, but abrogated BRCA1 recruitment by MYCN at all promoters tested (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), demonstrating that TFIIIC5 is required for MYCN-dependent recruitment of BRCA1 to multiple target sites.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP data in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TFIIIC5 is required for MYCN-dependent recruitment of BRCA1 to multiple target sites.
source: Depletion of TFIIIC5 had variable effects on the presence of BRCA1 by itself, but abrogated BRCA1 recruitment by MYCN at all promoters tested (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), demonstrating that TFIIIC5 is required for MYCN-dependent recruitment of BRCA1 to multiple target sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP experiments showing loss of MYCN-dependent BRCA1 recruitment upon TFIIIC5 depletion.

claim: TFIIIC is required for the association of the nuclear exosome with active promoters.
source: Collectively, the data show that TFIIIC is required for the association of the nuclear exosome and of BRCA1 with active promoters and that these effects are enhanced in cells expressing MYCN, arguing that they can account for the enhanced dependence of MYCN-expressing cells on TFIIIC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by CUT&RUN data showing decreased EXOSC5 association upon TFIIIC5 depletion.

claim: TFIIIC is required for the association of BRCA1 with active promoters.
source: Collectively, the data show that TFIIIC is required for the association of the nuclear exosome and of BRCA1 with active promoters and that these effects are enhanced in cells expressing MYCN, arguing that they can account for the enhanced dependence of MYCN-expressing cells on TFIIIC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP data showing loss of BRCA1 recruitment upon TFIIIC5 depletion.

claim: The effects of TFIIIC on exosome and BRCA1 association with promoters are enhanced in cells expressing MYCN.
source: Collectively, the data show that TFIIIC is required for the association of the nuclear exosome and of BRCA1 with active promoters and that these effects are enhanced in cells expressing MYCN, arguing that they can account for the enhanced dependence of MYCN-expressing cells on TFIIIC.
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 5B-C showing stronger effects in MYCN-expressing cells.

claim: The effects of TFIIIC on exosome and BRCA1 association can account for the enhanced dependence of MYCN-expressing cells on TFIIIC.
source: Collectively, the data show that TFIIIC is required for the association of the nuclear exosome and of BRCA1 with active promoters and that these effects are enhanced in cells expressing MYCN, arguing that they can account for the enhanced dependence of MYCN-expressing cells on TFIIIC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TFIIIC effects on exosome and BRCA1 are enhanced in MYCN-expressing cells.

claim: TFIIIC was first identified as a general transcription factor for RNAPIII.
source: TFIIIC was first identified as a general transcription factor for RNAPIII (Orioli et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TFIIIC binds to thousands of genomic sites that are not shared with RNAPIII and are called extra TFIIIC (ETC) sites.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Many ETC sites localise to RNAPII-transcribed promoters.

claim: TFIIIC is an architectural protein that can affect the three-dimensional chromatin organisation at its binding sites.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TFIIIC can act as insulator that blocks the spread of chromatin states.
source: Functionally, TFIIIC can act as insulator that blocks the spread of chromatin states (Raab et al., 2012), affect cohesin loading (Büchel et al., 2017), and bind at the borders of topologically associating domains (TADs) (Van Bortle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TFIIIC compartmentalises RNAPII promoters and gene expression.

claim: TFIIIC prevents the localisation of activity-dependent genes to sites of active transcription before stimulation.

claim: TFIIIC together with the activity-dependent neuroprotector homeobox protein controls the three-dimensional architecture of cell cycle genes.

claim: MYC and MYCN bind to virtually all active promoters.
source: Both MYC and MYCN bind to virtually all active promotors and profoundly alter the dynamics of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) transcription, with an increase in pause release and elongation being most apparent (Herold et al., 2019; Walz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MYC and MYCN profoundly alter the dynamics of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) transcription, with an increase in pause release and elongation being most apparent.

claim: MYC and MYCN control RNAPII function to limit the accumulation of R-loops.
source: Unrelated to those changes in gene expression, MYC and MYCN also control RNAPII function to limit the accumulation of R-loops, to facilitate promoter-proximal double-strand break repair and to coordinate transcription elongation with DNA replication (Papadopoulos et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MYC and MYCN facilitate promoter-proximal double-strand break repair.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MYC and MYCN coordinate transcription elongation with DNA replication.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Direct interactions of MYC and MYCN with MAX, WDR5, and MIZ1 control the localisation of MYC on chromatin.

claim: Both MYC and MYCN interact with and activate topoisomerases I and II.
source: Both MYC and MYCN also interact with and activate topoisomerases I and II, suggesting that MYC/N-dependent pause release also involves the relieve of torsional stress that builds up during early transcription (Das et al., 2022).

claim: MYC/N-dependent pause release involves the relief of torsional stress that builds up during early transcription.

claim: Both MYC and MYCN form prominent complexes with TFIIIC.
source: Intriguingly, both MYC and MYCN form prominent complexes with TFIIIC and mapping experiments for MYCN show that the amino-terminal transcriptional regulatory domain is required for the interaction (Büchel et al., 2017; Heidelberger et al., 2018).

claim: The three MYC paralogs (MYC, MYCN, and MYCL) are central players in normal development and tissue homeostasis.
source: The three MYC paralogs (MYC, MYCN, and MYCL) are central players in normal development and tissue homeostasis, and when dysregulated, fuel many of the processes that are hallmarks of cancer (Dhanasekaran et al., 2022; Hanahan, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When dysregulated, MYC paralogs fuel many of the processes that are hallmarks of cancer.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MYCN has a causal role in the development of neuroblastoma and other childhood tumours.
source: Among them, MYCN has attracted attention for its causal role in the development of neuroblastoma and other childhood tumours (Rickman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Active promoters coalesce at a discrete number of sites in the eukaryotic nucleus.
source: Active promoters coalesce at a discrete number of sites in the eucaryotic nucleus (Lim and Levine, 2021; Palacio and Taatjes, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many of the factors involved in basal transcription undergo liquid-liquid phase separation.
source: Many of the factors involved in basal transcription undergo liquid-liquid phase separation, arguing that transcription initiation takes place in condensate-like structures established by transcriptional regulatory domains and by RNAPII itself (Hnisz et al., 2017; Lewis et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Transcription initiation takes place in condensate-like structures established by transcriptional regulatory domains and by RNAPII itself.

evidence: This is inferred from the observation that transcription factors undergo phase separation.

claim: MYC proteins form condensates by themselves.
source: Consistent with their ubiquitous role in transcription, MYC proteins form condensates by themselves and enter condensates formed by the RNAPII-associated mediator complex (Boija et al., 2018; Solvie et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MYC proteins enter condensates formed by the RNAPII-associated mediator complex.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TFIIIC competes with the Aurora-A kinase for binding of MYCN.
source: Since TFIIIC competes with the Aurora-A kinase for binding of MYCN and Aurora-A in turn promotes elongation by RNAPII, we propose that the competition between both complexes enables transcriptional elongation on promoters that are activated by MYCN (Büchel et al., 2017; Roeschert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Aurora-A promotes elongation by RNAPII.
source: Since TFIIIC competes with the Aurora-A kinase for binding of MYCN and Aurora-A in turn promotes elongation by RNAPII, we propose that the competition between both complexes enables transcriptional elongation on promoters that are activated by MYCN (Büchel et al., 2017; Roeschert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The competition between TFIIIC and Aurora-A complexes enables transcriptional elongation on promoters that are activated by MYCN.
source: Since TFIIIC competes with the Aurora-A kinase for binding of MYCN and Aurora-A in turn promotes elongation by RNAPII, we propose that the competition between both complexes enables transcriptional elongation on promoters that are activated by MYCN (Büchel et al., 2017; Roeschert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is proposed based on the known competition and functions of TFIIIC and Aurora-A.

claim: The fate of nascent RNA is controlled by several interrelated processes leading to splicing and polyadenylation of the full-length transcript on the one hand, and mis-splicing, premature termination and RNA degradation on the other.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MYCN has been implicated in both splicing/polyadenylation and mis-splicing/premature termination/RNA degradation processes.

claim: The nuclear exosome is an RNA exonuclease complex that degrades multiple forms of aberrant nascent RNA.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: BRCA1 recruits the mRNA decapping enzyme DCP1 at promoters.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The TFIIIC/MYCN complex formation exerts a censoring and quality control function for RNAPII at promoters that have not received a full complement of activating signals.
source: We propose that the TFIIIC/MYCN complex formation exerts a censoring and quality control function for RNAPII at promoters that have not received a full complement of activating signals and hypothesise that this contributes to focus the transcription machinery and metabolic resources on the genes that drive the growth of MYCN-driven tumours.
evidence: This is proposed based on the collective findings of the study.
